# ROCOv2 — radiology images + captions

**Samples:** 24000 figure images from open-access biomedical papers
(PubMed Central), each paired with its **figure caption**, so row *i* is one
image–text pair (paired multimodal data).

| modality | kind | stored as |
|---|---|---|
| `image` | image | JPEG, RGB, shorter side resized to 256 px (aspect kept), path in column `image_path` |
| `text` | text | raw caption in column `caption` (median 17 words, 90th pct 38) |

Most images are grayscale scans stored as RGB. Captions are written by paper
authors for readers, not clinical reports: they often name the imaging
modality, body part and finding, and can mention arrows or panel letters.

## Labels (for evaluation)

- `label`: imaging modality, from ROCOv2's manually curated concepts
  (checked by a radiologist). Images with no or several modality concepts were
  dropped (see below).
- `cuis` / `concept_names`: all automatically extracted UMLS concepts of the
  caption (multi-label; usable as extra evaluation targets).

| label | train | val | test | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CT | 6998 | 791 | 717 | 8506 |
| X-ray | 5581 | 543 | 565 | 6689 |
| MRI | 3299 | 276 | 301 | 3876 |
| Ultrasound | 2746 | 283 | 322 | 3351 |
| Angiography | 1263 | 98 | 82 | 1443 |
| PET | 113 | 9 | 13 | 135 |

## Splits and subset

ROCOv2's own split (train / valid → `val` / test) is kept, so `test` images
come from different papers than `train`. A fixed random subset (seed 0)
of each split is used to keep training laptop-sized:

| split | available with one modality label | kept |
|---|---:|---:|
| train | 59465 | 20000 |
| val | 9773 | 2000 |
| test | 9822 | 2000 |

Fit every preprocessing step and model on `train` only; use `val` for model
choices and `test` for the final numbers.

## Modality concepts used for the label

| CUI | concept | label | images |
|---|---|---|---|
| C0040405 | X-Ray Computed Tomography | CT | 27747 |
| C1306645 | Plain x-ray | X-ray | 21997 |
| C0024485 | Magnetic Resonance Imaging | MRI | 12657 |
| C0041618 | Ultrasonography | Ultrasound | 11429 |
| C0002978 | angiogram | Angiography | 4799 |
| C0032743 | Positron-Emission Tomography | PET | 432 |

## Preparation already applied (not the agent's choice)

- Resizing (shorter side 256 px) and RGB conversion only; no cropping,
  no normalisation, no caption cleaning or tokenisation.

Source: https://zenodo.org/records/10821435 (CC BY-NC 4.0; non-commercial use only; individual images
keep the licences listed in ROCOv2's `license_information.csv`).

name: preprocessing
description: Choose a preprocess.py spec for each modality (encoder inputs and cross-modal prediction targets) from the profile, not from habit.
---

# When to apply
After the objective decision, before any training. One spec per modality for
the encoders; extra "target" specs only if the objective includes cross-modal
prediction. Log one `preprocessing` decision covering all specs, with the
`profile.json` numbers that justified each.

# Principles
- Everything fitted (feature selection, IDF, PCA/SVD, scaling) is fitted on
  train by the tool. You choose *what*, the tool guarantees *where*.
- Encoder inputs should be compact (tens to a few hundred dimensions) and
  denoised: contrastive encoders on 10⁴–10⁵ raw sparse features overfit and
  are slow.
- Read each `features/<mod>__<spec>.json` after running: dimension,
  explained variance, and for LSI `first_component_corr_with_depth`.

# Count modalities — decide from the profile

Read `profile.json → modalities.<m>`: `fraction_zero`, `library_size`,
`fraction_nonzero_values_equal_1`, `fraction_nonzero_values_le_2`,
`median_overdispersion_top2000`, `features_in_ge_1pct_samples`.

| Evidence | Data type it indicates | Encoder-input spec | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| counts spread over many values, overdispersed, ~10⁴ features (gene expression) | RNA-like | `log1p_hvg2000_pca50` (n_train < ~1,000: `hvg1000_pca30`) | library-size normalisation + log tames depth and skew; HVGs keep the informative genes; PCA denoises |
| ≥ ~0.7 of non-zero values ≤ 2, ≥ ~0.9 zeros, ~10⁵ features (peaks, accessibility) | near-binary, ATAC-like (10x counts each fragment's two cut sites, so "2" usually just means "open") | `tfidf_lsi50_drop1` | TF-IDF weights rare informative peaks; LSI is the standard reduction; the first component tracks sequencing depth |
| `drop1`: check `first_component_corr_with_depth` | | keep `drop1` if \|r\| ≳ 0.7; if \|r\| is small, rerun without it and log that | dropping a biological component would lose signal |
| very few features (< ~200) or already-reduced values | dense | `scale` (optionally `_pcaK`) | nothing to select |

Variants worth trying only if evaluation points to the input: more
components (`pca100`, `lsi100`) when the fine-label probe is far below the
coarse one; `log1p_scale_pca50` when a few very high-variance genes dominate.

## Cross-modal prediction targets (only if the objective asks)
Predict an interpretable, preprocessed version of the target modality — not
raw counts, not the target's own LSI/PCA (those are not "the modality"):
- RNA-like target: `log1p_hvg2000` (continuous; scored by Pearson r).
- ATAC-like target: `binary_top10000` (most-detected peaks, on/off; scored
  by AUROC). Use `binary_top5000` if n_train < ~2,000.

# Image and text modalities

| Situation | Spec | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A pretrained encoder exists whose training data matches the domain (e.g. BiomedCLIP for biomedical figures/captions) and both modalities have it | `biomedclip` for BOTH image and text | in-domain pretraining on far more pairs than we have; the two outputs already share a space, which gives a zero-shot baseline for free |
| Baseline to show what pretraining buys | text `tfidf_svd128`, image `pixels32_pca50` | deliberately simple; any learned model should beat them |
| Images mostly grayscale (`fraction_grayscale`) | no change — the pretrained encoder expects RGB, the tool converts | |

Pretrained features are computed once and cached (`outputs/_cache/`); a
second run with the same spec reads the cache in seconds. The first
encoding of tens of thousands of images can take many minutes on a laptop:
the tool prints progress with elapsed time — use the first lines to estimate
the total, run it in the background if it is long, and wait for the
`features/<mod>__biomedclip.npz` file. It does not count toward the training
budget.

Do NOT clean or mask caption text (e.g. removing modality words) unless the
objective asks for it — but record the text-shortcut number from the profile
(objective skill) because it changes how classification results are read.

1	---
2	name: objective
3	description: Turn the user's objective into downstream tasks, headline metrics, required baselines, a label-use policy and a falsifiable success criterion.
4	---
5	
6	# When to apply
7	Right after inspecting the data, before any preprocessing or modeling decision.
8	
9	# Step 1 — map the wording to downstream tasks
10	
11	| Objective wording | Downstream task | Headline metric (evaluate.py) | What it needs from the representation |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| "identify / classify / annotate cell types", "classify modality", "predict the label" | classification | `structure` → linear-probe **balanced accuracy** (and macro-F1) on the named label | a joint embedding (or the relevant modality's embedding) |
14	| "cluster", "discover groups", "unsupervised", "without labels" | clustering | `structure` → k-means **ARI / NMI**, silhouette | a joint embedding trained WITHOUT labels |
15	| "retrieve", "find the matching caption/image/cell", "search", "match across modalities" | cross-modal retrieval | `retrieval` → **recall@k** both directions, FOSCTTM | one embedding per modality in a SHARED space of equal dimension |
16	| "predict one modality from the other", "impute", "translate RNA→ATAC" | cross-modal prediction | `cross` → per-sample / per-feature Pearson r (continuous) or AUROC (binary) vs the train-mean baseline | an embedding of the SOURCE modality alone |
17	| "integrate", "joint representation", "combine modalities" | integration | classification/clustering of the joint embedding **vs each modality alone** | joint + per-modality embeddings |
18	| "does modality X add information?" | ablation | difference joint − best single modality, with CIs | single-modality baselines on the same split |
19	
20	An objective usually names two tasks; the first one named is primary.
21	If the objective asks for something no tool measures, say so, run the
22	closest supported analysis, and flag the gap in the report.
23	
24	# Step 2 — decide the label policy
25	
26	Labels in `dataset.json → label_columns` are first of all the *yardstick*.
27	
28	- **Default: no labels in training.** Train self-/cross-modally supervised
29	  methods (`clip`, `vicreg`, `simclr`, `pca_concat`, `identity`); evaluate
30	  with labels.
31	- **Labels allowed in training** (`supcon_clip`) only when the objective
32	  says labels are available for training, or explicitly asks for the best
33	  possible classifier. Then (a) keep a label-free model as the comparison,
34	  (b) mark every label-trained row as such, (c) never present its
35	  classification score as evidence of what the modalities share.
36	- **Check how the labels were made** (`DATA.md`). Labels predicted from ONE
37	  modality (e.g. cell types called from RNA alone) favour that modality's
38	  representation: a joint model can at best tie on them. Say this when you
39	  interpret "does adding modality X help?".
40	- **Text shortcut.** If `profile.json → modalities.<text>.label_predictable_from_words_alone`
41	  is high (≳ 0.8 balanced accuracy), classifying that label from the text side
42	  tests word-spotting, not representation quality: judge classification on the
43	  NON-text side (e.g. the image embedding) and treat retrieval as the
44	  alignment test.
45	
46	# Step 3 — fix the baselines before training
47	
48	Always: each modality alone (`pca_concat` with one input, or `identity` of a
49	pretrained encoder) and early fusion (`pca_concat` of all inputs). Add the
50	pretrained zero-shot embedding when a pretrained shared-space encoder exists
51	for these modalities. Chance levels come with every metric — quote them.
52	
53	# Step 4 — write the success criterion BEFORE training
54	
55	Log it as the `objective` decision: concrete, falsifiable, and achievable
56	with this test set (check class sizes in `profile.json → labels`; a class
57	with < ~10 test samples cannot carry a conclusion on its own). Examples:
58	
59	- integration: "the joint embedding's probe balanced accuracy on
60	  `label_fine` exceeds the best single modality's, with non-overlapping 95%
61	  CIs; otherwise report that the second modality adds no measurable label
62	  information";
63	- retrieval: "image→text recall@5 of the chosen model exceeds the zero-shot
64	  pretrained model's by more than the width of its 95% CI";
65	- prediction: "per-sample Pearson r of predicted vs observed target clearly
66	  above the train-mean baseline (CI excludes it)".
67	
68	Also state which label column is primary (fine-grained labels are more
69	informative about what a second modality adds than coarse ones, if their
70	classes are large enough), and what metric would make you change course.
71

---

# When to apply
Right after inspecting the data, before any preprocessing or modeling decision.

# Step 1 — map the wording to downstream tasks

| Objective wording | Downstream task | Headline metric (evaluate.py) | What it needs from the representation |
|---|---|---|---|
| "identify / classify / annotate cell types", "classify modality", "predict the label" | classification | `structure` → linear-probe **balanced accuracy** (and macro-F1) on the named label | a joint embedding (or the relevant modality's embedding) |
| "cluster", "discover groups", "unsupervised", "without labels" | clustering | `structure` → k-means **ARI / NMI**, silhouette | a joint embedding trained WITHOUT labels |
| "retrieve", "find the matching caption/image/cell", "search", "match across modalities" | cross-modal retrieval | `retrieval` → **recall@k** both directions, FOSCTTM | one embedding per modality in a SHARED space of equal dimension |

| "integrate", "joint representation", "combine modalities" | integration | classification/clustering of the joint embedding **vs each modality alone** | joint + per-modality embeddings |
| "does modality X add information?" | ablation | difference joint − best single modality, with CIs | single-modality baselines on the same split |

An objective usually names two tasks; the first one named is primary.
If the objective asks for something no tool measures, say so, run the
closest supported analysis, and flag the gap in the report.

# Step 2 — decide the label policy

Labels in `dataset.json → label_columns` are first of all the *yardstick*.

- **Default: no labels in training.** Train self-/cross-modally supervised
  methods (`clip`, `vicreg`, `simclr`, `pca_concat`, `identity`); evaluate
  with labels.
- **Labels allowed in training** (`supcon_clip`) only when the objective
  says labels are available for training, or explicitly asks for the best
  possible classifier. Then (a) keep a label-free model as the comparison,
  (b) mark every label-trained row as such, (c) never present its
  classification score as evidence of what the modalities share.
- **Check how the labels were made** (`DATA.md`). Labels predicted from ONE
  modality (e.g. cell types called from RNA alone) favour that modality's
  representation: a joint model can at best tie on them. Say this when you
  interpret "does adding modality X help?".
- **Text shortcut.** If `profile.json → modalities.<text>.label_predictable_from_words_alone`
  is high (≳ 0.8 balanced accuracy), classifying that label from the text side
  tests word-spotting, not representation quality: judge classification on the
  NON-text side (e.g. the image embedding) and treat retrieval as the
  alignment test.

# Step 3 — fix the baselines before training

Always: each modality alone (`pca_concat` with one input, or `identity` of a
pretrained encoder) and early fusion (`pca_concat` of all inputs). Add the
pretrained zero-shot embedding when a pretrained shared-space encoder exists
for these modalities. Chance levels come with every metric — quote them.

# Step 4 — write the success criterion BEFORE training

Log it as the `objective` decision: concrete, falsifiable, and achievable
with this test set (check class sizes in `profile.json → labels`; a class
with < ~10 test samples cannot carry a conclusion on its own). Examples:

- integration: "the joint embedding's probe balanced accuracy on
  `label_fine` exceeds the best single modality's, with non-overlapping 95%
  CIs; otherwise report that the second modality adds no measurable label
  information";
- retrieval: "image→text recall@5 of the chosen model exceeds the zero-shot
  pretrained model's by more than the width of its 95% CI";
- prediction: "per-sample Pearson r of predicted vs observed target clearly
  above the train-mean baseline (CI excludes it)".

1	---
2	name: fusion
3	description: Choose how to combine the modalities (no fusion, early fusion, aligned shared space, supervised alignment, light fine-tuning of a pretrained model), the encoder, and what to compare it against.
4	---
5	
6	# When to apply
7	After preprocessing, before choosing hyperparameters. Log one `fusion`
8	decision (strategy + baselines) and one `model_selection` decision (method +
9	encoder) — or a single `fusion` decision if they are inseparable.
10	
11	# The options (train.py --method)
12	
13	| Method | What it does | Lecture idea | Gives per-modality embeddings in one space? | Uses labels? |
14	|---|---|---|---|---|
15	| `pca_concat` (1 input) | single-modality baseline: PCA of one modality | PCA | — | no |
16	| `pca_concat` (all inputs) | early fusion: z-score, weight modalities equally, concatenate, PCA | PCA / early fusion | no (joint only) | no |
17	| `identity` | use a pretrained encoder's features as they are | foundation model, zero-shot | yes, if the encoder was trained jointly (e.g. BiomedCLIP image + text) | no |
18	| `clip` | one encoder per modality; paired samples pulled together, other pairs in the batch pushed apart (symmetric InfoNCE) | contrastive / CLIP (L23–L24) | yes | no |
19	| `vicreg` | one encoder per modality; paired embeddings close + each dimension keeps variance + dimensions decorrelated; no negatives | non-contrastive SSL (L24) | yes | no |
20	| `supcon_clip` | `clip` + supervised contrastive term: same-label samples are also positives | SupCon (L23) | yes | **yes** |
21	| `simclr` | ONE modality, two augmented views of each sample | SSL (L24) | — | no |
22	
23	Encoders (`--encoder`): `mlp` (default for inputs from PCA/LSI/TF-IDF),
24	`linear` (tiny n, or to test whether nonlinearity matters), `adapter`
25	(residual MLP starting at the identity: light fine-tuning of pretrained
26	features; requires input dim = `--dim`, e.g. 512 for BiomedCLIP).
27	
28	# Decision rules
29	
30	**1. Always build the baselines** (objective skill): each modality alone and
31	`pca_concat` of all inputs; `identity` of the pretrained features when they
32	exist. They cost seconds.
33	
34	**2. Pick the primary method from the objective and the data:**
35	
36	| Situation (evidence) | Primary | Why / alternative worth one comparison |

# When to apply
After preprocessing, before choosing hyperparameters. Log one `fusion`
decision (strategy + baselines) and one `model_selection` decision (method +
encoder) — or a single `fusion` decision if they are inseparable.

# The options (train.py --method)

| Method | What it does | Lecture idea | Gives per-modality embeddings in one space? | Uses labels? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pca_concat` (1 input) | single-modality baseline: PCA of one modality | PCA | — | no |
| `pca_concat` (all inputs) | early fusion: z-score, weight modalities equally, concatenate, PCA | PCA / early fusion | no (joint only) | no |
| `identity` | use a pretrained encoder's features as they are | foundation model, zero-shot | yes, if the encoder was trained jointly (e.g. BiomedCLIP image + text) | no |
| `clip` | one encoder per modality; paired samples pulled together, other pairs in the batch pushed apart (symmetric InfoNCE) | contrastive / CLIP (L23–L24) | yes | no |
| `vicreg` | one encoder per modality; paired embeddings close + each dimension keeps variance + dimensions decorrelated; no negatives | non-contrastive SSL (L24) | yes | no |
| `supcon_clip` | `clip` + supervised contrastive term: same-label samples are also positives | SupCon (L23) | yes | **yes** |
| `simclr` | ONE modality, two augmented views of each sample | SSL (L24) | — | no |

Encoders (`--encoder`): `mlp` (default for inputs from PCA/LSI/TF-IDF),
`linear` (tiny n, or to test whether nonlinearity matters), `adapter`
(residual MLP starting at the identity: light fine-tuning of pretrained
features; requires input dim = `--dim`, e.g. 512 for BiomedCLIP).

# Decision rules

**1. Always build the baselines** (objective skill): each modality alone and
`pca_concat` of all inputs; `identity` of the pretrained features when they
exist. They cost seconds.

**2. Pick the primary method from the objective and the data:**

| Situation (evidence) | Primary | Why / alternative worth one comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Paired samples, objective includes retrieval or cross-modal prediction, no pretrained shared-space encoder | `clip` with `mlp` encoders | a shared space is required; contrastive alignment is the standard way to get it. Alternative: `vicreg` |
| Same, but small n_train (< ~2,000) or many near-duplicate pairs (duplicate texts, cells of one type that look alike) | `vicreg` | contrastive loss treats look-alike pairs as negatives (false negatives) and is batch-size hungry; VICReg has no negatives. Alternative: `clip` with a smaller batch |
| A pretrained encoder already maps both modalities into one space (`identity` works: retrieval well above chance on val) | `clip` with `--encoder adapter --select-by val_recall` on the pretrained features (= light fine-tuning) | starts exactly at the zero-shot model, and epoch 0 is kept unless an epoch beats it on val matching, so it can only end at or above the zero-shot model on val; cheap. Alternative: `mlp` projection heads on the same features (more capacity, more overfitting risk) |
| Objective is only integration/classification and modalities are unpaired or retrieval is irrelevant | `pca_concat` may already be enough — test `clip`/`vicreg` joint against it | a learned method is justified only if it beats early fusion |
| Objective explicitly allows labels for training | `supcon_clip` next to the label-free primary | report both; the label-free one answers "what do the modalities share?" |
| Only one modality has signal for the objective (e.g. single-modality baseline ≈ joint everywhere) | say so; keep the multimodal model only if it adds retrieval/prediction | |

**3. Embedding size** (`--dim`): ~ the number of meaningful directions —
16–64 for cell types (tens of classes), the pretrained dimension (512) for
an adapter. Bigger is not better for contrastive training at n ~10⁴.

as a logged iteration that a specific val result motivated.

  embedding computed as their average then mixes two offsets — compare the

3	description: Choose which evaluate.py tasks measure the objective, compare models on val, report on test, and interpret every metric against its baseline and chance level.
4	---
5	
6	# When to apply
7	After training (on val, to choose), after the choice (on test, to report),
8	and when writing the results section.
9	
10	# Pick tasks from the objective
11	
12	| Objective task (objective skill) | `--tasks` | extra flags |
13	|---|---|---|
14	| classification / integration | `structure,collapse` | `--labels` all label columns; read the primary one first |
15	| clustering | `structure,collapse` | look at ARI/NMI and silhouette, not the probe |
16	| retrieval | `retrieval,collapse` | (+ `structure` if classification is also asked) |
17	| cross-modal prediction | `cross` | `--cross a->b:<target spec>,b->a:<target spec>` (targets from preprocessing) |
18	
19	Run the SAME tasks on every model and baseline, so `compare_runs.py` can
20	put them side by side. `cross` needs the run to contain an embedding of the
21	source modality (`z_<src>`): the single-modality baseline of the source gives
22	the non-multimodal reference ("how well does RNA alone, compressed the same
23	way, predict ATAC?").
24	
25	# Val to choose, test to report
26	1. `evaluate.py --split val` for every model → `compare_runs.py --split val`
27	   → choose. Log the choice with the val numbers.
28	2. `evaluate.py --split test` for the chosen model(s) AND the baselines →
29	   `compare_runs.py --split test --reference <best single-modality baseline>`
30	   (and once more with `--reference <early fusion or zero-shot>` if that is the
31	   stronger baseline for a claim) → these numbers go in the report.
32	If test disagrees with val (e.g. ranking flips within overlapping CIs), say
33	so — do not switch models because of it.
34	
35	# Reading each metric
36	
37	**Classification (`structure`)**
38	- *Probe balanced accuracy*: a linear classifier on the embedding (fit on
39	  train). Balanced = mean recall over classes, so a majority class cannot
40	  hide failures on rare ones. Compare with `chance_balanced_accuracy` and
41	  the single-modality baselines. Use `probe_per_class_recall` to name the
42	  classes a representation fails on.
43	- *kNN balanced accuracy*: does the neighbourhood structure (not just a
44	  linear direction) carry the label?
45	- **"Is A better than B?" is answered by the PAIRED difference**
46	  (`comparison_<split>_vs_<reference>.md`): both models are scored on the same
47	  samples, so resampling them together removes the shared sample-to-sample
48	  noise. Overlapping per-model intervals are NOT evidence of no difference —
49	  never conclude "no proven gain" from them. Report the difference with its CI
50	  ("+0.05 [+0.02, +0.08]"), and judge size as well as sign: with thousands of
51	  samples a tiny difference (e.g. +0.004 in per-cell r) can exclude 0 and still
52	  be practically irrelevant — say so.
53	- Small classes dominate the noise of balanced accuracy (each class weighs
54	  the same): name classes with < ~10 evaluated samples as uninterpretable.
55	- **Name the weakest LARGE class**: from `probe_per_class_recall`, the class
56	  with the most samples among those with low recall (e.g. < 0.75). A big
57	  class that is often misclassified matters more to users than a tiny one,
58	  and it usually points to biologically/visually similar neighbours.
59	- Labels made from one modality (DATA.md) cap what the other can add —
60	  read "joint ≈ that modality alone" as expected, not as failure.
61	- Text shortcut: if the label is predictable from words alone
62	  (`profile.json`), the text embedding's probe is not evidence of anything —
63	  and neither is the JOINT probe, because the joint embedding averages in the
64	  text. Report the non-text side: the `probe_bal_acc[<label>](image)` column
65	  of `comparison_<split>.md` and the "(image)" rows of the paired table. Do not
66	  put text-only baselines in a column about classifying from the image.
67	- `compare_runs.py` shows the joint probe AND each modality's own probe for
68	  multimodal models (column suffix "(rna)", "(image)", ...). Choose the column
69	  that answers the objective's question and name it in the report.
70	
71	**Clustering**: ARI (0 = random, 1 = identical to labels) and NMI; kmeans
72	uses k = number of classes, so very imbalanced labels depress ARI even for a
73	good embedding — interpret with the probe. Even when the objective does not
74	ask for clustering, mention it if the chosen model's ARI is clearly the
75	worst of the compared models: it means classes are linearly separable but not
76	grouped into compact clusters, which matters to anyone who will cluster the
77	embedding.
78	
79	**Retrieval (`retrieval`)**: recall@k = fraction of queries whose true partner
80	is in the top k out of `n_candidates`; chance is k / n_candidates. Report
81	both directions; asymmetry is normal. FOSCTTM = average fraction of
82	candidates closer than the true partner (0 perfect, 0.5 random) — the most
83	stable single number for paired cells. Exact-duplicate texts (profile
84	`duplicate_text_fraction`) put a small ceiling on text-side recall@1.
85	For paired single cells, recall@1 is naturally low (thousands of cells of the
86	same type look alike); FOSCTTM and recall@10 are the better summaries.
87	
88	**Cross-modal prediction (`cross`)**
89	- Continuous target: *per-sample Pearson r* (does the predicted profile of a
90	  cell correlate with its observed one?) compared with
91	  `per_sample_pearson_baseline_train_mean` — the baseline is high because all
92	  cells share an average profile, so the GAIN over it is the result; *per-
93	  feature r* (does a gene's predicted level track its observed level across
94	  cells? baseline 0) and `r2_vs_baseline`.
95	- Binary target: per-feature AUROC (baseline 0.5) and per-sample AUROC vs the
96	  train-mean baseline.
97	
98	**Collapse / geometry (`collapse`)**: effective rank ≪ dim or `dead_dims` > 0
99	→ partial collapse (training skill). `alignment_paired_sq_dist` should be far
100	below `alignment_random_pairs_sq_dist`. `modality_gap_centroid_dist` > ~0.5
101	means two separate clouds (see fusion skill).
102	
103	**Figures**: `embedding.png` (test) — left: joint embedding coloured by the
104	primary label; right: both modalities in the shared space with grey lines
105	joining a few pairs. Describe what is visible (separated classes? mixed
106	modalities or two clouds?). `comparison_<split>.png` for the report.
107	
108	# When evaluation should trigger an iteration
109	- A learned model is below its own baselines on the primary metric → check
110	  training health first; then try the logged alternative.
111	- Fine-label probe far below coarse-label probe while coarse is near perfect
112	  → more input components (preprocessing skill) or larger `--dim`.
113	- Retrieval far above chance but classification below baselines → the joint
114	  embedding (average of modalities) may be hurt by a modality gap: compare
115	  per-modality probes, and consider using the best modality's embedding.
116	- Adapter never beats zero-shot on val → stop; zero-shot is the answer.
117	  A very strong zero-shot baseline leaves little headroom: judge a gain
118	  against the zero-shot CI, and remember it may be inflated by pretraining
119	  overlap (recommendation skill).

good embedding — interpret with the probe. Even when the objective does not
ask for clustering, mention it if the chosen model's ARI is clearly the
worst of the compared models: it means classes are linearly separable but not
grouped into compact clusters, which matters to anyone who will cluster the
embedding.

is in the top k out of `n_candidates`; chance is k / n_candidates. Report
both directions; asymmetry is normal. FOSCTTM = average fraction of
candidates closer than the true partner (0 perfect, 0.5 random) — the most
stable single number for paired cells. Exact-duplicate texts (profile
`duplicate_text_fraction`) put a small ceiling on text-side recall@1.
For paired single cells, recall@1 is naturally low (thousands of cells of the
same type look alike); FOSCTTM and recall@10 are the better summaries.

**Cross-modal prediction (`cross`)**

  cell correlate with its observed one?) compared with
  `per_sample_pearson_baseline_train_mean` — the baseline is high because all
  cells share an average profile, so the GAIN over it is the result; *per-

  cells? baseline 0) and `r2_vs_baseline`.

  train-mean baseline.

below `alignment_random_pairs_sq_dist`. `modality_gap_centroid_dist` > ~0.5
means two separate clouds (see fusion skill).

primary label; right: both modalities in the shared space with grey lines
joining a few pairs. Describe what is visible (separated classes? mixed
modalities or two clouds?). `comparison_<split>.png` for the report.

  embedding (average of modalities) may be hurt by a modality gap: compare
  per-modality probes, and consider using the best modality's embedding.

  A very strong zero-shot baseline leaves little headroom: judge a gain
  against the zero-shot CI, and remember it may be inflated by pretraining
  overlap (recommendation skill).

name: recommendation
description: Run and report the downstream analyses the objective asked for, then give one consistent recommendation of which representation to use, for what, and with which caveats.
---

# When to apply
After the test evaluation of the chosen model(s) and baselines.

# Downstream analyses
The objective names them (objective skill); each gets its own report
subsection with: the question in plain words, the method in one sentence
(e.g. "a linear classifier trained on the embeddings of training cells"),
the headline number next to its baseline and chance, the 95% CI, and one
sentence of interpretation. At least one downstream analysis is required.

| Downstream task | Evidence to show |
|---|---|
| classification | probe balanced accuracy (+ macro-F1) for chosen model vs every baseline; the 2–3 classes it handles best/worst (`probe_per_class_recall`) |
| clustering | ARI/NMI vs baselines; the embedding figure |
| retrieval | recall@1/5/10 both directions vs chance and vs zero-shot; one sentence on what a miss tends to look like if visible (e.g. same modality, different body part) |
| cross-modal prediction | per-sample r / AUROC vs the train-mean baseline and vs the single-modality baseline embedding; per-feature r and the fraction of features predicted with r > 0.3 |

Log one `downstream` decision summarising the analyses run and their headline
numbers (with file names).

# The recommendation (log `recommendation`)
Answer the objective in one sentence, then:

1. **Which representation, for which use.** It can differ by task — e.g.
   "joint VICReg embedding for cell-type annotation; the RNA encoder alone
   when only RNA is measured" or "fine-tuned adapter for retrieval; the
   zero-shot model is within its CI for modality classification".
2. **The deciding numbers**: the chosen model vs the best baseline on the
   primary metric, as a PAIRED difference with its 95% CI
   (`comparison_test_vs_<baseline>.md`), next to the two values.
3. **Verdict categories** (pick one, use it in the header, Summary and
   Recommendation):
   - *Multimodal helps*: the chosen multimodal representation beats the best
     single-modality / zero-shot baseline on the primary metric, with a paired
     difference whose CI excludes 0 and a size that matters.
   - *Multimodal enables*: no gain on classification, but it provides
     something a single modality cannot (retrieval, cross-modal prediction).
   - *No measurable gain*: the paired difference vs the best baseline has a CI
     that includes 0 (or is too small to matter) — recommend the simpler
     baseline (fewer moving parts), and say what evidence would change this.
   - *Can't tell*: the test set cannot resolve the question (too few samples
     in the relevant classes); say which data would.
4. **Caveats that change how to use it**: label provenance (labels predicted
   from one modality), text shortcuts, label-trained models, duplicates,
   subset size, one donor / one data source, and **pretraining overlap**: if
   a pretrained encoder was trained on data from the same source as this
   dataset (compare `DATA.md` source with what is known about the encoder's
   pretraining data), its zero-shot scores — and anything built on them — may
   be inflated by having seen test samples. State it as a possibility unless
   the overlap can be ruled out; it cannot be measured with these tools.
5. **What would change the recommendation** (one or two concrete items).

Implementation matters: prefer the simplest representation whose paired
difference from the best includes 0 — a frozen pretrained model or PCA is
easier to deploy and audit than a trained encoder.

# Naming numbers consistently
A model with several embeddings (joint, plus one per modality) yields
several "RNA" numbers. In the Summary, Results and Recommendation, "RNA
alone" / "image alone" always means the single-modality BASELINE model. If
you also discuss a multimodal model's own per-modality embedding (e.g. its
RNA encoder), name it explicitly ("the joint model's RNA encoder") and never
put it where a baseline number is expected. The comparison table and the
prose must show the same numbers for the same names.

Writes O/features/<modality>__<spec>.npz (X: [all samples, d], float32) and a
.json next to it (what was done, dims, fit statistics). Every learning method in
tools/train.py reads these matrices, so the spec is THE preprocessing decision.
Any fitted step (feature selection, IDF weights, PCA/SVD, scaling) is fitted on
the train split and then applied to val/test.

Spec = steps joined by "_", applied left to right.

counts modalities (raw counts):
  log1p        normalise each sample to 10,000 total counts, then log(1+x)
  tfidf        term-frequency x inverse-document-frequency, then log(1+1e4*x)
               (standard for sparse, near-binary data such as ATAC peaks)
  binary       x > 0 -> 1
  hvgN         keep the N most variable features (dispersion within mean bins)
  topN         keep the N features detected in the most train samples
  scale        z-score each feature (clipped at +-10)
  pcaK         PCA to K components
  lsiK         truncated SVD to K components, each component z-scored
  drop1        drop the first SVD/PCA component (in TF-IDF/LSI it mostly tracks

# generated_report_2: ROCOv2 radiology figures — shared image–caption space for retrieval and modality classification

**Verdict:** No measurable gain from training: the frozen, pretrained BiomedCLIP model already matches captions to images and identifies the imaging modality best, and our fine-tuning could not improve on it (it may be flattered by having seen this kind of data).

## 1. Summary

- **Question:** Can we learn a shared image–caption representation that retrieves the right caption for an image (and vice versa) and classifies imaging modality from the image?
- **Approach:** Compared frozen BiomedCLIP, two light fine-tunes of it (no labels used in training), and simple pixel / word-count baselines.
- **Result:** Frozen BiomedCLIP puts the true caption in the top 5 of 2,000 for 81% of images (chance 0.25%) and classifies modality from the image with 0.972 balanced accuracy; fine-tuning did not beat it.
- **Recommendation:** Use the frozen BiomedCLIP image and text encoders for retrieval, and its image encoder with a linear classifier for modality; no training needed.

## 2. Data at a glance

- Two modalities on the same 24,000 figures: the image (median 296×256 px, 70% grayscale) and its caption (median 16 words). Split 20,000 train / 2,000 validation / 2,000 test; test papers differ from train papers.
- Label: imaging modality, 6 classes (CT, X-ray, MRI, Ultrasound, Angiography, PET). The test set is 36% CT; PET has only 13 test images and is too few to interpret alone.
- Captions often give the label away: a classifier on words alone reaches 0.91 balanced accuracy (chance 0.17), so classification is judged from the image side only.

![Class counts, example images and caption lengths](../outputs/generated_report_2_rocov2/profile.png)

## 3. Decision path

EOF
cat $O/decision_path.md >> $R
cat >> $R <<'EOF'

The turning point was step 5: training the light fine-tune made the training loss fall but the matching of captions to images on validation data got worse, so the original pretrained model was kept — twice.

## 4. Methods compared

- **BiomedCLIP zero-shot** — the pretrained biomedical image and text encoders used as they are; they already share one space.
- **Fine-tuned BiomedCLIP** (not tested separately) — a small correction layer started at the pretrained model, trained to improve matching. Two learning rates were tried; both ended at the unchanged pretrained model, so on test it is identical to zero-shot.
- **Retrained projection (MLP)** — new two-layer networks trained from scratch on the BiomedCLIP features with a contrastive objective (matching pairs pulled together).
- **Image alone / text alone** — simple features (32×32 pixels or word TF-IDF) reduced by PCA to 32 dimensions.
- **Early fusion** — those two simple feature sets concatenated and reduced to 32 dimensions.

No labels were used for training. Models were chosen on validation; the test set was scored once for the models above. The single-modality and early-fusion baselines have no shared space, so they cannot retrieve.

## 5. Results

Test set, 2,000 images. "Image→caption" asks: for an image, is its caption among the top 5 of 2,000 candidates (chance 0.25%)? Modality classification uses the image embedding alone (chance 0.167).

| Model | Image→caption top-5 | Caption→image top-5 | Modality from image (balanced acc.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| BiomedCLIP zero-shot | 0.808 | 0.808 | 0.972 |
| Retrained projection (MLP) | 0.675 | 0.682 | 0.973 |
| Image alone (pixels, PCA) | – | – | 0.605 |
| Early fusion (joint embedding; image-only score not defined) | – | – | 0.694 (joint) |
| Text alone (words, PCA; joint embedding) | – | – | 0.730 (text; not valid evidence for images) |

Paired differences against zero-shot (95% CI):
- Retrained projection, image→caption: −0.133 [−0.152, −0.114]; caption→image: −0.126 [−0.146, −0.108] — clearly worse.
- Retrained projection, modality from image: +0.001 [−0.006, +0.008] — no difference.
- Image alone: −0.367 [−0.391, −0.343] — far worse.

![Test comparison across models](../outputs/generated_report_2_rocov2/comparison_test.png)

The bars show the pretrained models and the retrained projection far above the simple baselines for classification, and the pretrained zero-shot highest for both retrieval directions; blank bars mean the baseline does not provide that quantity.

## 6. Downstream analyses

### 6.1 Retrieving the right caption (and image)
A caption (or image) is the query; we rank all 2,000 test partners by cosine similarity. For zero-shot, the true caption is first for 50% of images (top 5: 81%, 95% CI 79–82%; top 10: 88%) and the median rank is 2; the reverse direction is the same (top 5: 81%). Chance for top 5 is 0.25%. The retrained projection is 13 points lower. Images of the same modality are easy to confuse; the embedding figure shows class structure but we did not inspect individual misses.

### 6.2 Classifying modality from the image
A linear classifier trained on training-set image embeddings. Zero-shot image embeddings give 0.972 balanced accuracy (95% CI 0.964–0.979; chance 0.167). Recall is ≥ 0.965 for Angiography, CT, MRI and Ultrasound; X-ray is the weakest large class (0.904, 565 images). PET (13 images) is not interpretable alone.

![Test embedding of zero-shot BiomedCLIP: classes (left), image and caption clouds (right)](../outputs/generated_report_2_rocov2/biomedclip_zeroshot/embedding.png)

Left: classes form distinct groups, with X-ray the most spread out and PET a tiny cluster. Right: images and captions sit in two separate clouds (centroid distance 0.80), yet retrieval still works because the nearest caption is chosen by ranking.

## 7. Recommendation

Use the **frozen BiomedCLIP** encoders as the shared image–caption representation: for retrieval (top-5 about 0.81 each way) and, via its image embedding with a linear classifier, for modality classification (0.972). Fine-tuning gave no gain (adapter runs reverted to the pretrained model; the retrained projection is 0.13 worse at retrieval and equal for classification, difference +0.001 [−0.006, +0.008]). Verdict: no measurable gain from training; the simpler frozen model is preferred.

Caveats: BiomedCLIP was pretrained on figure–caption pairs from PubMed Central, the same source as ROCOv2, so its scores may be inflated by overlap — this cannot be measured here. The label (modality) is often named in the caption, so text-side classification is not evidence. What would change this: a test on figures from outside PubMed Central, or fine-tuning with far more data or compute than the 20-minute budget (only about 1 minute was used).

## 8. Limitations

- Only a 20,000-pair training subset and 2,000-image test set; PET has 13 test images.
- Two learning rates were tried for the light fine-tune and one setting for the retrained projection; other settings may behave differently.
- Retrieval among 2,000 candidates is easier than among a full archive.
- The fine-tune runs were not scored on test because they equal zero-shot by construction (validation numbers are identical).
- Misses were not inspected visually.

## Appendix A. Full decision log

EOF
cat $O/decisions.md >> $R
cat >> $R <<'EOF'

## Appendix B. Training details

| Run | Settings | Minutes | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fine-tune (adapter), lr 1e-4 | 512-d, batch 512, up to 8 min | 0.23 | epoch 0 kept; early stop at epoch 20; val top-1 0.623 before and after |
| Fine-tune (adapter), lr 1e-5 | same, up to 4 min | 0.21 | epoch 0 kept; val top-1 0.623 |
| Retrained projection (MLP) | 2 layers × 512, dropout 0.2, lr 1e-3, batch 512, up to 5 min | 0.41 | best epoch 27 of 47; val top-1 0.503; val loss rose after the best epoch (overfitting) |

Total training time about 0.9 minutes of the 20-minute budget (plus brief smoke tests). Health checks: no collapse (no dead dimensions; effective rank 33 for the MLP); matching far above chance (val top-1 chance 0.0005). Loss curves: `outputs/generated_report_2_rocov2/clip_mlp_d512/loss.png`.

## Appendix C. Glossary

- **Top-5 recall (recall@5):** share of queries whose true partner is among the 5 highest-ranked of 2,000 candidates.
- **Balanced accuracy:** mean of the per-class recalls, so rare classes count equally.
- **Linear probe:** a linear classifier fitted on frozen embeddings.
- **Zero-shot:** using the pretrained model with no training on this data.
- **Adapter / fine-tune:** a small trainable correction on top of pretrained features.
- **Contrastive (CLIP) training:** pulling matched image–caption pairs together and pushing others apart.
- **PCA / TF-IDF:** simple dimension reduction / word-weighting.
- **Paired bootstrap CI:** confidence interval for a difference, resampling the same test samples for both models.
- **Modality gap:** images and captions occupying separate regions of the shared space.
- **Early fusion:** concatenating features from both modalities and reducing them together.

## Appendix D. Reproduce

EOF
cat $O/commands.md >> $R
/usr/bin/python3 tools/export_report.py $R | tail -3

## Appendix C. Glossary

- **Top-5 recall (recall@5):** share of queries whose true partner is among the 5 highest-ranked of 2,000 candidates.
- **Balanced accuracy:** mean of the per-class recalls, so rare classes count equally.
- **Linear probe:** a linear classifier fitted on frozen embeddings.
- **Zero-shot:** using the pretrained model with no training on this data.
- **Adapter / fine-tune:** a small trainable correction on top of pretrained features.
- **Contrastive (CLIP) training:** pulling matched image–caption pairs together and pushing others apart.
- **PCA / TF-IDF:** simple dimension reduction / word-weighting.
- **Paired bootstrap CI:** confidence interval for a difference, resampling the same test samples for both models.
- **Modality gap:** images and captions occupying separate regions of the shared space.
- **Early fusion:** concatenating features from both modalities and reducing them together.

**Decision:** Frozen BiomedCLIP is the representation to use, and training did not improve on it. The verdict in the report is "no measurable gain from training". No labels were used in training.

**Test results** (2,000 images, 2,000 candidate captions; numbers from `comparison_test.md` and `comparison_test_vs_biomedclip_zeroshot.md`):

| Model | Image→caption top-5 | Caption→image top-5 | Modality from image (balanced acc.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| BiomedCLIP zero-shot | 0.808 | 0.808 | 0.972 |
| MLP projection heads trained from scratch on BiomedCLIP features | 0.675 | 0.682 | 0.973 |
| Pixel-PCA image alone | – | – | 0.605 |

- **Retrieval:** chance for top-5 is 0.0025. The retrained heads are worse than zero-shot by −0.133 [−0.152, −0.114] image→caption and −0.126 [−0.146, −0.108] caption→image.
- **Modality classification:** the retrained heads match zero-shot (+0.001 [−0.006, +0.008]). The pixel baseline is far worse (−0.367 [−0.391, −0.343]).
- **Fine-tuning:** both light fine-tunes of BiomedCLIP (learning rates 1e-4 and 1e-5) ended at the unchanged pretrained model. Validation matching got worse as training loss fell. I did not score them on test, since they are identical to zero-shot.
- **Budget:** about 0.9 of the 20 minutes was used.

**Caveats:**
- BiomedCLIP was pretrained on PubMed Central figure–caption pairs, the same source as ROCOv2, so its scores may be inflated. This can't be measured with these tools.
- Captions often name the modality (words alone give 0.91 balanced accuracy), so classification is judged from the image side only.
- PET has 13 test images and can't be interpreted on its own.
